edges.description: APC loss establishes the WNT-dysregulated background on which acquired KRAS and BRAF alterations cooperate to shape invasion and therapy response.
edges.source: APC Loss in Intestinal Stem Cells

edges.description: Loss of GUCY2C tumor-suppressive signaling removes a brake on crypt proliferation, permitting adenoma-to-carcinoma progression.
Cooperating WNT and RAS signalling drives the invasive programs by which tumour cells detach from the primary epithelium and breach stromal barriers.
Colonising tumour cells engage hepatic stromal populations, including cancer-associated fibroblasts, that create a permissive metastatic niche.
Hepatic micrometastases drive angiogenic remodelling to sustain vascular adaptation and outgrowth at the secondary site.
Cells that have detached from the epithelial matrix must survive that detachment to persist during portal transit.
Detachment-resistant cells persist in the portal circulation long enough to arrest and colonise the liver, the dominant first metastatic site.

nodes.description: Wnt-pathway-activating loss of APC in intestinal stem cells drives early neoplasia.
nodes.id: APC Loss in Intestinal Stem Cells

evidence.reference_title: Crypt stem cells as the cells-of-origin of intestinal cancer.
evidence.snippet: Intestinal cancer is initiated by Wnt-pathway-activating mutations in genes such as adenomatous polyposis coli (APC).

nodes.description: Stepwise progression from adenomatous polyps to invasive carcinoma drives colon adenocarcinoma development.

evidence.reference_title: The adenoma carcinoma sequence in colorectal neoplasia.
evidence.snippet: Molecular studies support the clinical impression that adenocarcinoma of the large intestine develops in stages. At the center of the pathological continuum between normal mucosa and invasive carcinoma is the premalignant lesion, the adenomatous polyp.

nodes.description: Metastatic colorectal cancer promotes angiogenic remodeling at secondary sites to sustain micrometastatic survival, vascular adaptation, and outgrowth in the hepatic microenvironment.

evidence.reference_title: Proteomic landscape of colorectal cancer liver metastasis.
evidence.snippet: MM tumors exhibited suppressed ferroptosis and activation of the TGF-β signaling pathway, while SM tumors displayed inhibited anoikis and activation of the WNT signaling pathway, accompanied by activated angiogenesis.

nodes.description: A subset of metastatic colorectal cancers survives matrix detachment during transit, allowing circulating or portal-disseminating cells to persist long enough to seed the liver and other distant niches.

evidence.reference_title: Proteomic landscape of colorectal cancer liver metastasis.
evidence.snippet: MM tumors exhibited suppressed ferroptosis and activation of the TGF-β signaling pathway, while SM tumors displayed inhibited anoikis and activation of the WNT signaling pathway, accompanied by activated angiogenesis.

nodes.description: Low-dose aspirin is an established chemopreventive ("interception") agent that reduces the recurrence of colorectal adenomas — the precursor lesions of colon adenocarcinoma. The cited randomized trial evaluated secondary prevention in higher-risk individuals with a recent history of documented adenomas; the 81 mg dose reduced adenoma recurrence while 325 mg did not. Its antineoplastic effect in the large bowel is attributed largely to inhibition of COX/prostaglandin-driven pro-tumorigenic signaling within the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Preventive use is balanced against gastrointestinal bleeding risk.

evidence.reference_title: A randomized trial of aspirin to prevent colorectal adenomas.
evidence.snippet: We performed a randomized, double-blind trial of aspirin as a chemopreventive agent against colorectal adenomas.

nodes.description: Metastatic colorectal cancer cells detach from the primary epithelium, invade through vascular and stromal barriers, and colonize the liver through a stepwise dissemination program consistent with EMT-linked invasive plasticity.

evidence.snippet: Metastasis of the liver from colorectal cancer represents the final stage of a multistep biological process.

nodes.description: Oral GUCY2C agonists (linaclotide, plecanatide) aim to reactivate the tumor-suppressive GUCY2C axis that is silenced early in colorectal carcinogenesis, restoring cGMP-dependent homeostatic signaling and restraining epithelial proliferation. In a human study oral linaclotide activated GUCY2C and reduced colorectal epithelial proliferation, but only after colon preparation — the FDA-approved gastric-release formulation does not reliably reach the colorectum, so a colorectum-targeted formulation is required before this can serve as a chemopreventive.

evidence.reference_title: Bioactivity of Oral Linaclotide in Human Colorectum for Cancer Chemoprevention.
evidence.snippet: The study results highlight the importance of developing a novel GUCY2C agonist formulated for release and activity targeted to the large intestine for colorectal cancer prevention

nodes.description: The intestinal receptor guanylyl cyclase C (GUCY2C) enforces epithelial homeostasis and restrains crypt proliferation. Early in colorectal carcinogenesis its endogenous hormones guanylin and uroguanylin are lost, silencing GUCY2C-cGMP signaling and removing a tumor-suppressive brake — a change that permits progression along the adenoma-carcinoma sequence and is the rationale for GUCY2C-agonist chemoprevention.

evidence.reference_title: Bioactivity of Oral Linaclotide in Human Colorectum for Cancer Chemoprevention.
evidence.snippet: Guanylate cyclase C (GUCY2C) is a tumor-suppressing receptor silenced by loss of expression of its luminocrine hormones guanylin and uroguanylin early in colorectal carcinogenesis.

nodes.description: The liver is the dominant first metastatic site because colorectal venous drainage enters the portal circulation and because hepatic stromal, endothelial, and immune niches support tumor cell arrest and outgrowth.

evidence.snippet: The liver is the first location of metastatic disease; due to that the main mechanism of dissemination is through the portal system.

nodes.description: MUC1 is an epithelial glycoprotein aberrantly expressed on colorectal adenomas and carcinomas, making it a candidate shared antigen for immunoprevention. A MUC1 peptide vaccine aims to raise anti-MUC1 immunity to intercept recurrent adenoma formation in individuals with a prior advanced adenoma. In a randomized, placebo-controlled prevention trial the vaccine was immunogenic only in vaccine recipients but did not significantly reduce adenoma recurrence overall; a 38% absolute reduction was seen in the subset who mounted an immune response. It remains investigational.

evidence.reference_title: Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial of MUC1 Peptide Vaccine for Prevention of Recurrent Colorectal Adenoma.
evidence.snippet: An immune response was observed only in vaccine recipients.

nodes.description: Metastatic outgrowth depends on reciprocal signaling between tumor cells and stromal populations such as cancer-associated fibroblasts, which help create a permissive hepatic microenvironment and immunosuppressive niche.

evidence.reference_title: A dual-targeting strategy to inhibit colorectal cancer liver metastasis via tumor cell ferroptosis and cancer-associated fibroblast reprogramming.
evidence.snippet: Within the "seed and soil" paradigm, disrupting both tumor cells and their supportive microenvironment is essential to suppress disease progression.

nodes.description: Metastatic colorectal cancer typically evolves on a background of APC/WNT pathway dysregulation, with KRAS and BRAF alterations shaping invasion, therapy response, and liver metastatic fitness. These pathways reinforce proliferative signaling and resistance to anoikis during dissemination.

evidence.reference_title: Prognostic value of KRAS and BRAF mutations in curatively resected colorectal cancer.
evidence.snippet: KRAS and BRAF mutations are associated with inferior survival, independent of MSI status, in Japanese patients with curatively resected CRC.
